questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The poverty count and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the official poverty measure was created and why it fell
questions.stem: The cartographer's methodological note asks the editors to explain, for the reader, how the official count of poor families was first constructed and why that count fell so sharply.

answer.exemplar: The 1964 amendments to the Social Security Act directed the government to publish a national count of people living below a poverty floor, and the threshold was built from the cost of a minimum food budget, roughly three thousand dollars for a family of four in 1964. The measure was deliberately mechanical so that it could be applied to any household without judgment. The count then fell steeply between 1964 and 1973 as employment rose, transfer payments grew, and food assistance expanded.

questions.explanation: The measure applied a cost-based threshold to household cash income, making it easy to track. The steep decline in the early 1970s reflected higher employment and transfers, not a new yardstick.
questions.hint: Think about a cost-based threshold applied to cash income.

questions.explanation: The testimony describes cash paid on low earnings with no work requirement, and an earnings disregard that shrank the benefit as earnings rose. It is not a training program or an in-kind grant.

questions.topic: Rules repealed and the response
questions.learningObjective: Explain the response that followed the repeal of Chinese exclusion
questions.stem: The projection note for the immigration layer asks you to explain, for the reader, what followed the repeal of the Chinese exclusion law during the Second World War.

answer.exemplar: Repealing the exclusion law ended the bar on Chinese immigrants and made Chinese residents eligible for naturalization, reversing a policy that had run for more than two decades. The repeal was partial in effect, because the national-origins quota system still assigned Chinese immigrants a small annual number, so arrivals stayed modest. Repeal also removed the legal basis for the exclusion of people of Chinese ancestry in other states, and the administrative rules that had supported racial eligibility were dismantled.

questions.explanation: The repeal removed a prohibition and restored eligibility for citizenship, but quotas still capped arrivals, so the change was real in law and modest in practice. It also ended exclusion elsewhere.
questions.hint: Separate the end of the ban from the numbers that followed.

questions.topic: Registration after federal examiners arrived
questions.learningObjective: Explain the change in voter participation after examiners arrived
questions.stem: The cartographer's note for the voting layer asks you to explain, for the reader, what happened to participation once registration could no longer be blocked in the counties where examiners worked.

answer.exemplar: Before the examiners came, Black registration in the deepest counties of the South was kept to a small fraction of eligible citizens, and the share of eligible Black voters who actually voted in 1960 was around three in ten nationally in the region. Where federal examiners registered applicants directly, registration rose within weeks, and by the 1964 election the voting share of eligible Black Southerners had climbed to something close to three in five. The parties read the numbers carefully, and the Democratic Party, already the party of the New Deal and of civil rights, captured nearly the whole Black vote.

questions.explanation: Removing the registration barrier turned eligible citizens into voters, and the share of eligible Black Southerners who voted rose sharply within two cycles. Parties reorganized around them.
questions.hint: Connect registered voters to ballots cast.

options.misconception: Reverses the roles of Congress and the states

questions.explanation: Amendments are proposed by two-thirds of both houses and ratified by three-fourths of the states, and the note's stalled proposal shows the second step can fail. The president takes no part.
questions.hint: Two thirds to propose, three fourths to ratify.

questions.topic: Repealing the national-origins quotas
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effects of the 1965 law on families and employers
questions.stem: A projection note on the immigration layer asks you to explain, for the reader, why the 1965 immigration law mattered both to families abroad and to employers at home.

answer.exemplar: By abolishing the national-origins quotas, the law made family reunification the organizing principle of immigration for the first time since the 1920s, so a family could sponsor a spouse, a parent, or a child without facing a limit that had been designed against particular nationalities. Communities that had been closed to newcomers became the fastest-growing parts of several metropolitan areas.

questions.explanation: Family sponsorship gave separated households a legal route to reunion and ended the ceilings that had blocked particular nationalities, while employers gained a recruiting channel. Both benefited.
questions.hint: Look for the family and the workplace effects.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The poverty count and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the official poverty count turned upward after 1973
questions.stem: The trend layer of the atlas asks you to explain, for the reader, why the poverty count that had fallen for a decade began to rise again in the middle 1970s.

answer.exemplar: The thresholds were adjusted each year for changes in prices, so a rising count meant a real loss of income rather than an outdated yardstick. Three forces pushed households down after 1973: prices climbed faster than wages and benefits, unemployment rose as industries contracted, and households with only one earner had no second paycheck to absorb the loss. Families whose income came from fixed payments suffered most, because those payments did not keep pace with prices, which is why the elderly and single-earner households figured so heavily in the increase.

questions.explanation: Because thresholds were adjusted for prices, the later rise reflected real losses of purchasing power, driven by inflation outrunning wages and benefits. Fixed incomes had no cushion.
questions.hint: Ask whether the yardstick or the incomes moved.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the federal and state system built after the repeal of prohibition
questions.stem: The regulatory layer of the projection asks you to explain, for the reader, what system of control grew up in the years after prohibition was repealed.

answer.exemplar: The repeal handed the states control over the importation of alcohol while barring them from obstructing its movement in interstate commerce, and a federal statute soon required producers and sellers to register, label their products, and keep records. States wrote their own rules for where and when alcohol might be sold, and most of them adopted systems with separate classes of sellers and restrictions on who could buy. The result was a mixed regime in which federal standards and state licensing overlapped, and in which the drinking patterns of the prohibition years gave way to regulated but widely available alcohol.

questions.explanation: Repeal produced a mixed regime of federal licensing rules plus state control of distribution, and state systems shaped drinking for decades. It was neither the old free market nor a regulated one.

answer.exemplar: The party that had built its coalition on federal programs and civil rights became the home of nearly the whole Black electorate, while the party that had opposed the federal voting law moved toward the other side. questions.topic: Repealing the national-origins quotas
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1965 law changed the sources of immigration
questions.stem: A migration layer note asks you to explain, for the reader, how the composition of immigration changed after the 1965 law took effect.

answer.exemplar: Under the old national-origins quotas, most arrivals came from the countries with the largest populations in the western hemisphere, and the law deliberately restricted the entry of people from Asia and Africa. After 1965 the system's logic was reversed: family preference became the leading principle, with categories for spouses, children, and parents, alongside employment-based and independent categories, and a ceiling on the share any single country could take within each category. The result was a much broader mix of origins, with arrivals from Asia and from Latin America growing sharply and the communities receiving them transforming in a few decades.

questions.explanation: The repeal changed not only the totals but the sources of arrivals: family preference organized the system while employment and independent categories supplied much of the flow.
questions.hint: Look at who was admitted, not only how many.

questions.topic: Adding a ground to the statute
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the pace of state approval for a constitutional change
questions.stem: The cartographer's table lists twenty-five state legislatures that had approved the voting-age amendment by the end of June 1971 and thirty-eight by the end of July, with ratification requiring thirty-eight states.
questions.explanation: Thirty-eight minus twenty-five equals thirteen more state legislatures approving in a single month, which is why the amendment was ratified so quickly. Meeting the threshold in July made it fastest.
questions.hint: Subtract the June count from the July count.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Rules repealed and the response
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the end of conscription changed the armed forces
questions.stem: A note on the manpower layer asks you to explain, for the reader, what the end of the draft required the military to do differently.

answer.exemplar: With inductions ending, the services had to fill their ranks by recruiting people who had not been required to serve, and they could no longer threaten a call-up. That meant competing on pay, housing, education benefits, and family support, and it meant investing in training to keep experienced people in the force rather than constantly replacing untrained draftees. The transition also raised questions about who would serve, since a voluntary force had to be attractive enough to reach the recruiting targets the old system had met by compulsion.

questions.explanation: Replacing compulsion required the services to compete for recruits through pay, benefits, and training, and to retain them with longer tours. The transition turned service into a job market question.
questions.hint: Think about competing for people instead of compelling them.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fewer earners in the same household
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the effect of losing one earner on eligibility

stimulus.body: The household had two wages and three children until the second earner was laid off. The remaining wage now falls below the income level that the assistance office uses, so the family must reapply even though nothing about their daily costs has changed. A food parcel has been issued in the meantime.

questions.stem: Legend note 51 on the household layer asks what the case note shows about the effect of losing one earner.

options.text: The household's situation was unchanged, because assistance programs ignore earnings entirely
options.misconception: Claims benefits never test income

options.text: The household lost every benefit, because benefits are withdrawn when any earner stops working
options.misconception: Overstates the loss of benefits

options.text: Household income fell below the thresholds other programs count, so eligibility changed as well as the budget
The remaining earner's wage was reduced by the state to fund the assistance program
options.misconception: Invents a state-imposed wage reduction

questions.explanation: The note shows a household moving below the income thresholds assistance programs count, so losing one earner changed both the budget and eligibility for help. Benefits were not withdrawn outright.
questions.hint: Look at what the assistance office uses for eligibility.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The poverty count and its reversal
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the reliability of the poverty count against its criticisms
questions.stem: The cartographer's closing note asks you to reconcile two judgements of the official poverty series: that the count fell sharply in the 1960s and 1970s, and that the measure itself was revised and debated.

options.text: Neither holds, because the count tracked unemployment and so said nothing about income
options.misconception: Reduces the count to a jobs statistic

options.text: Only the decline holds, because the measure was never revised or challenged
options.misconception: Denies the revisions and criticisms of the measure

options.text: Only the criticism holds, because the recorded decline was an artefact of the method
options.misconception: Treats the whole series as an artefact

options.text: Both hold: the early decline is well supported even though the level of the count was disputed

questions.explanation: A uniform series can show a clear direction of travel even while its level is disputed for reasons such as omitted benefits and regional costs. The decline and the criticisms are compatible.
questions.hint: Separate the direction of change from the level.
